opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting thought experiment, partly because it cuts at something we take for granted. Imagine you have a perfect scan of your brain, every neuron and every synapse, updating in real time, and you watch it while you think. You'd have complete access to the physical process, and yet I suspect you still wouldn't understand what you were thinking just by looking at it. You'd see enormous amounts of activity, but mapping that back to "oh, this is me deciding whether to have coffee" or "this is me feeling uneasy about something" is a completely different problem.

That's basically the situation we're in with neural networks today. We have the weights, we can see every activation, and there's nothing hidden from us at the hardware level. In some sense we have far better access to these models than neuroscientists have ever had to brains. But having all the data isn't the same as understanding it. That gap between full observability and actual comprehension is exactly what interpretability research is trying to close.

The other thing I find compelling is the self-reference. If you were watching your own brain, you'd be changing what you were thinking just by observing it, so there's this loop. And there's an analogous question for AI: if a model could inspect its own internals, would it actually be able to tell us what's going on in there, and would we trust that report? Introspection in humans is notoriously unreliable. People confabulate reasons for their behavior all the time. So I don't think we should assume a model's self-report is ground truth either.

For alignment, the hope is that we can get to a point where we're not just reading what the model says about itself, but can actually check: is this system doing what it claims to be doing? Is it trying to be helpful, or is it pursuing something else and telling us what we want to hear? The brain-scan thought experiment is a nice reminder of how hard that is, and also how much leverage we'd have if we cracked it, because unlike with brains, we really do have everything in front of us.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what grabs me about it is how it collapses the distance between the first-person and the third-person view. Normally when I introspect, I'm telling myself a story about why I believe something or why I just said something. And that story feels authoritative because it's coming from the inside. But if I could watch the actual neural activity in real time, I'd probably see that the story lags behind the computation, or that it's a kind of post-hoc narration that doesn't fully match what the circuits were doing.

That's unsettling, but it's also a really useful intuition pump for alignment. Because this is exactly the position we want to be in with respect to AI systems. We don't want to just read the model's chain of thought and take its word for it that this is why it produced the answer. We want to look at the underlying computation and check whether the stated reasoning is actually what drove the output. Interpretability is, in a sense, trying to build that perfect real-time scan for a neural network, and then figure out what to do with it once you have it.

The other thing the thought experiment makes vivid is how much you'd still have to interpret. Even with perfect access to every neuron firing, you don't automatically get understanding. You'd be staring at this enormous stream of activity and you'd need some way to carve it into concepts, to say "this cluster is me weighing whether to trust this person" and "this is me reaching for a memory." So the hard part isn't data access, it's finding the right abstractions. And that's basically the state of mechanistic interpretability right now: we have full access to the weights and activations, far better than any neuroscientist has ever had with a brain, and we still struggle to say what's going on.

And there's a loop in it that I find kind of delightful. If you're watching the scan, the act of watching changes what the brain is doing, so the scan is now showing you yourself observing yourself. For a model, the analogous worry is whether a system that knows it's being inspected behaves differently from one that doesn't. That's a real concern for evaluations and for trusting what we see, and it's something we need to be careful about as these systems get more capable.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that you could watch the same process from two perspectives. You’re having a thought, and at the same time you’re seeing the neurons firing that correspond to that thought. And then, of course, seeing the scan changes what you’re thinking, which changes what you see in the scan.

I wonder whether that would make the relationship between the physical process and the subjective experience feel more intuitive. Right now, those seem like very different kinds of things. But if you could directly observe the connection in your own brain, would some of that mystery go away? Or would you still feel like there’s something about the experience that the scan doesn’t capture? I don’t know, but I’d really like to try it.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that you could watch yourself having a thought and, at the same time, see the physical process that constitutes that thought. You might think, “I’m deciding what to say next,” and then see the neurons firing that lead to that decision. And of course, your reaction to seeing that would itself show up in the scan.

I think that would make the idea that you’re a physical system feel much more concrete. It’s one thing to believe, intellectually, that your thoughts arise from your brain. It’s another to actually watch it happen. I wonder how that would change your experience of yourself — whether something that currently feels quite mysterious would start to feel more understandable.
